title: How do you engage in conversation with your casual movie going friends or family?

commenti.body:
Critic is a job, isn’t it, not something you decide for yourself.

Talk to people how they want to be talked to. If your family don’t like what you like, find others to talk to.

Honestly, if you want to be an ‘intellectual’ or just learned in a field, setting aside condescension and ego is a good first step.

Maybe don't talk at length with such people about movies? There are many other conversational topics to choose from. And they'd probably rather focus on other stuff anyway. In general it's bad form to shit on people's opinions. If they liked a movie you hated, maybe find out what they liked about it and move on. File the data away in your brain. Maybe you can offer your opinion or have a debate. Read the room. And be open to thoughts and interpretations you hadn't had. Be open to reconsidering your own views. You never know where insight might come from.

All depends on the context. I will watch just about anything and find things to like. I’d rather have pleasant conversations with friends and family than put them down for liking a certain movie when movies aren’t really one of their interests.

I ask them what their favorite movies are, and then I try to think of movies of similar genre/type that I think are especially good. I ask if they've seen them, and we can either talk about them if they have, or I recommend they do if they haven't.

I do love me some steak, but sometimes what I absolutely crave us a cheap burger, even amongst the dross you can find the odd gem.Try appreciating a movie for what it's intended to be, not everything has to be an experimental arthouse film from 1950s communist Yugolslavia about the existential dread felt by the common man as expressed through the plight of urban fox's in the aftermath if War, sometimes a good fart gag can be just the palette cleanser you need.

lifetime movies are awesome tho

maybe treat these big dumb movies as if they are comedies first. and generally look at their positives instead of picking apart their flaws

I just don’t. My thoughts on cinema or television are no better than my family or friend’s. They are jjst “thoughts”. 

While my daily work as a filmmaker, does give me greater insight, those insights primarily serve my own inner creative world. I find that anything I have to “say” about film is better to be channeled through my own work. If i just start talking deeply about other films with people who don’t care to the same degree that I care, it typically won’t move the needle for them, and could make them feel alienated, as if I’m trying to recruit a disinterested person into a religion. See what I mean? 


Ultimately there is nothing that interesting about being a consumer. It’s a personal experience for everyone. It’s like… “I don’t want to know your deep feelings about the local pizza place, aside from the basic is it “good” or “bad” - just let me make up my own mind. It’s like that. However, if I make the movie, ad, etc, then the person I’m sharing it with will care, because they know me, and this is my work. 

At the end of the day we don’t “know” Tarkovsky or Wong Kar Wai, and it’s weird to speak about them with familiarity. But using the medium of film to self express and share our own creativity-a genuine part of ourselves-with family and friend is a great bonding experience.

I personally won't try to force discussion on a topic that just doesn't interest the other person all that much, completely shitting on another person's taste is a surefire way to get them to never engage with you on the topic again. I just try to point out the positives in the 'bad' movies and maybe give a recommendation of a similar movie that the other person might be able to enjoy.

i try to avoid it, even what they are big film lovers. it seems like it breeds resentment and they take it personally. i find many people who love movies, aren't usually reading opinions that conflict heavily with their own. i always liked to explore the full breadth of the discourse.

It's entirely up to them to enjoy whatever they want. You shouldn't be too snobbish and dismissive of other people's tastes. You seem to be approaching this by tring to prove them wrong, but there are no right or wrong answers. The way to engage with them is by recommending some of your favorites and seeing how they respond to them.
